quote: Ferner wenn man eine beliebige geschlossene Raumcurve mit beliebigen vielfachen Punkten giebt; giebt es dann immer eine [-Fläche-] geschlossene im Endlichen liegende reguläre singularitätenfreie Fläche, die diese [-...-] geg. Raumcurve als Doppelcurve hat
english: Further, if an arbitrary closed space curve with arbitrary multiple points is given, is there always a closed, regular, singularity-free surface lying in the finite region that has this given space curve as its double curve?
topic: The page ends a note on a surface problem with a reference to Bianchi's theorem that fundamental quantities determine a surface, then asks whether a fixed family of closed curves bounds the true convergence region of expansions in a given series of analytic functions, and closes with questions inspired by Boy's surface: a 3-dimensional image of projective space in 4-space, and surfaces having a prescribed space curve as double curve.

triage.modern_statement: Let C be a closed curve in R^3. It may be a single component or several, and it may cross itself at any number of points with any multiplicity. Is there always a closed surface F and a smooth immersion f: F -> R^3, meaning a regular map with no singular points and bounded image, whose double-point set (self-intersection curve) is exactly C? Put another way: which space curves, possibly with multiple points, can be the double curve of an immersed closed surface? Boy's surface, an immersion of RP^2 with one triple point and a double curve in three loops, is the example Hilbert had in mind.
triage.answered_by: I found no source that answers Hilbert's question as he stated it (any closed space curve with any multiple points). Related work exists on parts of it. T. Banchoff (1974) showed that the number of triple points of a general-position immersed surface is congruent mod 2 to its Euler characteristic, which limits the double curves that can occur. B. Kalmár (arXiv 1704.05823) characterized which systems of disjoint circles in S^2 can be the multiple-point set of a generic immersion S^2 -> R^3. That result is about the preimage in the surface, not about a given curve in space. There is also extensive work on double-point curves of surface-knot diagrams. My searches were cut off by a tool-use limit, so a direct treatment may exist that I did not find.

evidence.claim: Banchoff showed that the number of triple points of an immersed surface in general position is congruent mod 2 to the surface's Euler characteristic. This is a known constraint on how double curves can be arranged.

Kalmár characterizes which unions of disjoint embedded circles in S^2 can be the multiple-point set of a generic immersion of S^2 into R^3, in terms of how the circles interlace. This is a modern answer to a closely related realization question.

In the modern setting, the double-point set of an immersed closed surface in R^3 is studied as a family of generically immersed closed curves (double-decker sets), with Boy's surface as a standard example.
Double-point curves of immersed surfaces (surface-knot diagrams) are still being studied, for example in work on triple point numbers.
Recent work studies the double-point curves of triple-point-free immersed spheres and cites Banchoff on triple points and surgery of immersed surfaces.

triage.why: This is a real research question: it asks which space curves can be the self-intersection curve of an immersion. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source that names or answers it in his general form. The sources only cover nearby results, Banchoff's parity theorem and Kalmár's characterization in the surface, which show that double curves of generic immersions cannot be arbitrary. One further point is my own reasoning and is not stated in any source I found. In a generic immersion, the double curve meets itself only at triple points, where three branches cross. A curve with a plain two-branch crossing therefore seems to fail for generic immersions. Non-generic immersions, with tangential contact between sheets, could allow more cases, so the answer depends on how the question is made precise. Double-point curves of immersed surfaces are an active topic, but I can't confirm that this specific realization question is being worked on.
